'''''Heliotropium arborescens''''', the '''garden heliotrope''' or just '''heliotrope''', is a [[species]] of flowering plant in the family [[Heliotropiaceae]], native to [[Bolivia]], [[Colombia]], and [[Peru]]. Common names also include '''cherry pie''' and '''common heliotrope'''.<ref name=RHSAZ>{{cite book | editor-last = Brickell | editor-first = Christopher | title = The Royal Horticultural Society A-Z Encyclopedia of Garden Plants | year = 2008 | page = 519 | publisher = Dorling Kindersley | location = United Kingdom | isbn = 9781405332965}}</ref>

==Description==
Growing to {{convert|1.2|m|ft|abbr=on}} tall and broad, it is a bushy, [[evergreen]], short-lived shrub with dense clusters of bright purple flowers, notable for their intense, rather [[vanilla]]-like fragrance.<ref name="PFAF">{{Cite web|url=https://pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Heliotropium+arborescens|title=Heliotropium arborescens Heliotrope, Garden heliotrope, Cherry Pie, Heliotrope PFAF Plant Database|website=pfaf.org}}</ref> Like many borage plants, the vanilla flower also contains poisonous [[pyrrolizidine alkaloid]]s in addition to the fragrances.

== Distribution and habitat ==
The species is native to [[Bolivia]], [[Colombia]], and [[Peru]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Heliotropium arborescens - Plant Finder |url=http://www.missouribotanicalgarden.org/PlantFinder/PlantFinderDetails.aspx?kempercode=a513 |access-date=2021-02-25 |website=www.missouribotanicalgarden.org}}</ref>

== Cultivation ==
As a perennial, it is hardy in [[Hardiness zone|zones]] 10 to 11, and requires wintering indoors in zones 9 or colder.<ref name="NCSUedu">{{Cite web|title=Heliotropium arborescens (Heliotrope, Peruvian Heliotrope) {{!}} North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox|url=https://plants.ces.ncsu.edu/plants/heliotropium-arborescens/|access-date=2021-02-25|website=plants.ces.ncsu.edu}}</ref> It is hardy down to about {{convert| 5|C|F|abbr=on}}. It can also be grown as a [[hardiness (plants)|half-hardy]] [[annual plant|annual]] (grown from seed under glass and planted out after all danger of frost has passed) in those areas.<ref name=clausen/> Alternatively soft-wood cuttings may be taken in summer.<ref name=RHSAZ/>

During the Victorian era in [[England]] this plant gained great recognition,{{citation needed|date=October 2025}} often appearing in gardens and the [[herbaceous]] borders of parks. They were also grown as standards.<ref name=clausen>{{cite book| title=Essential Perennials: The Complete Reference to 2700 Perennials for the Home Garden |publisher=Timber Press | year=2015 | url= https://books.google.com/books?id=5-ZmBgAAQBAJ&q=Heliotropium+arborescens&pg=PA208 | page=208 | isbn= 9781604696721| author=	Ruth Rogers Clausen, Thomas Christopher}}</ref>  A vanilla-scented heliotrope was laid on the coffin of the American poet [[Emily Dickinson]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.telegraph.co.uk/gardening/3343213/New-feet-within-my-garden-go.html|title=New feet within my garden go|website=www.telegraph.co.uk}}</ref> Note that the common name "garden heliotrope" may also refer to [[valerian (herb)|valerian]],<ref>{{GRIN | name = Valeriana officinalis | id = 400139}}</ref> which is not closely related.

===Cultivars===
Its popularity may have become less in more modern times, but hardy and colourful [[cultivar]]s, such as 'Princess Marina', have ensured that this plant still regularly appears in seed catalogues and garden centres.  Other popular cultivars include, 'Mary Fox', the highly scented 'White Lady' or 'White Queen' and the taller 'Florence Nightingale'.
*'Fragrant delight' has more fragrant purple flowers, and leaves with purple highlights.<ref name=clausen/>
*'Marine' has large highly fragrant dark purple flowerheads to 15 cm (6 in) diameter, and burgundy leaves.<ref name=clausen/>
*'Sweet heaven' has paler fragrant flowers and is more heat-tolerant.<ref name=clausen/>
*'White' has flowers that smell of almonds.<ref name=clausen/>

‘Chatsworth’<ref name = RHSPF>{{cite web | url=https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/91160/i-Heliotropium-arborescens-i-Chatsworth/Details
| title = RHS Plantfinder - ''Heliotropium arborescens'' 'Chatsworth' | accessdate=3 March 2018}}</ref> and 'Princess Marina',<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/95812/Heliotropium-arborescens-Princess-Marina/Details | title = ''Heliotropium arborescens'' 'Princess Marina' | publisher = RHS | accessdate = 6 August 2020}}</ref> both strongly scented with deep purple flowers, have gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web  
| url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants - Ornamental | date = July 2017 
| page = 47 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | accessdate = 2 March 2018}}</ref>

==Toxicity==
The seeds are poisonous.<ref name=PFAF/> The [[American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals|ASPCA]]'s Animal Poison Control Center article on heliotropes lists them as a substance which is toxic to horses and can induce liver failure in equines.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Heliotrope|url=https://www.aspca.org/pet-care/animal-poison-control/toxic-and-non-toxic-plants/heliotrope|access-date=2021-02-25|website=ASPCA|language=en}}</ref> The plant is not very palatable, but will be eaten by animals with no other forage; poisonings typically occur from ingestion of green plant material or material in hay.

The toxic components can cause liver failure, referred to as "walking disease" or "sleepy staggers". Signs include weight loss, weakness, sleepiness, yawning, incoordination, yellowish discoloration to mucous membranes (icterus), neurologic problems secondary to liver failure (aimless walking, chewing motions, [[head pressing]]).{{Citation needed|date=February 2021}} Animals may appear to be normal at first, then become suddenly affected; the syndrome progresses rapidly over a few days to a week.

[[Pyrrolizidine alkaloid]]s often cause upset stomachs and liver damage for humans who ingest any part of the plant.<ref name="NCSUedu" />

The purple coloration of the flower lent itself to the so-called "heliotrope [[cyanosis]]" that was characteristic of severely ill patients in the [[Spanish flu|1918 flu pandemic]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Honigsbaum|first=Mark|date=June 2018|title=Spanish influenza redux: revisiting the mother of all pandemics|journal=The Lancet| volume=391| issue=10139| pages=2492–2495| doi=10.1016/s0140-6736(18)31360-6| pmid=29976462|s2cid=49709093| issn=0140-6736}}</ref>
